entrenched

/en-TRENCHT/ - rhymes with drenched · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Entrenched means firmly established and difficult to change.

Tipping is so entrenched in American restaurants that every attempt to swap it for a service charge has quietly fizzled.

Example

The QWERTY keyboard was laid out in the 1870s, partly to keep a mechanical typewriter's arms from jamming. The jamming arms are gone; the layout is not. Provably faster arrangements have been designed, marketed, and forgotten for a century, because the cost of retraining every typist on earth defeats every argument. QWERTY is entrenched — not best, just dug in.

Entrenched is the exact word because it names what is firmly established and difficult to change — a practice that has dug fortifications, so that challenges break against it. The military picture is the point: entrenched things are not merely old or common; they are defended by habit, cost, and inertia. You don't tidy an entrenched arrangement away. You campaign against it, and usually lose.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ingrained: Ingrained habits are worked into the grain of a person or a culture by years of repetition — quiet, internal, second nature. Entrenched points outward: a practice that has dug defenses and beats back open attempts to change it. Ingrained explains why you keep doing it; entrenched explains why reformers keep failing.

deep-rooted: Deep-rooted describes what long years have anchored far below the surface, like a tree grown down through decades. Entrenched adds the military picture: not only old or deep, but actively defended, so that campaigns against it break and fail. Deep-rooted measures age and depth; entrenched measures resistance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shaky: barely holding, easy to dislodge

fluid: still able to flow into a new shape

Where it sits · how hard it is to dislodge

accepted → entrenched → unshakable

accepted vs. entrenched: An accepted practice has merely won agreement; an entrenched one has dug in and repels attempts to change it.

unshakable vs. entrenched: Unshakable goes past entrenched — no argument, cost, or campaign will ever move it at all.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-: in, into

Root — trench: a dug ditch (French trenchier, 'to cut')

Suffix — -ed: having been

Put it together: En- (into) + trench (a dug ditch) + -ed (having been) = having been dug into a trench. Soldiers entrench by cutting defensive ditches into the earth and settling in behind them. The borrowed sense keeps the soldiers' logic: whatever is entrenched has fortified its position and expects to outlast any attack.

Use the root in a new word: trench: The crew cut a trench along the road to lay the new water pipe.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / journalistic

Entrenched is the reporter's word for practices, beliefs, and interests that have dug in against change — use it when reform keeps failing. This unit's conventionally describes the accepted way of doing things; a convention becomes entrenched precisely when attempts to change it start breaking against the habit. For roots-and-character images, ingrained is the gentler cousin.
